\begin{abstract}
 Passive Optical Network (PON) is a widely deployed fiber access technology. While major PON standards from ITU-T encrypt the payload, frame headers are still plaintext, and recent work has shown that header fields such as the payload length indicator (PLI) can be exploited to infer encrypted user activity. This paper proposes \textbf{SecurePON},  a security-enhanced PON architecture that periodically rotates the XGEM Port-ID via the OMCI channel and bursts cover traffic on expired Port-IDs to prevent an adversary on the splitter from tracking per-ONU traffic.
\end{abstract}

\section{Introduction}
Passive Optical Network (PON) is widely deployed in FTTx access networks and in cellular (LTE, 5G) X-haul networks~\cite{front}.
Given popular deployment of PON, protecting user traffic confidentiality in PON is essential. 
However, major PON protocols standardized by ITU-T support only payload encryption, not header encryption. Recent work has shown that the resulting plaintext headers can be exploited to infer user activity~\cite{PLI}.


The privacy implications extend beyond per-frame inference. Because the XGEM Port-ID identifying each logical connection is typically static after provisioning, an adversary on the splitter can group PLI observations per ONU and build per-ONU traffic datasets.


In this paper, we propose \textbf{SecurePON}, a security-enhanced PON architecture based on Higher Speed PON (HSP)~\cite{itu-50GPON}. SecurePON periodically rotates the XGEM Port-ID assigned to each ONU via the OMCI channel and bursts cover traffic on expired Port-IDs to prevent an adversary on the splitter from tracking per-ONU traffic. SecurePON reuses functions already defined
in Higher Speed PON Specifications. Therefore, It is very compatible with deployed PON infrastrcutres.

\section{Background}

\subsection{PON Topology}

In a major PON architecture~\cite{itu-g9843,itu-XGPON,itu-XGSPON,itu-NGPON2,itu-50GPON}, an Optical Line Terminal (OLT), located at the Central Office (C.O.), is connected to multiple Optical Network Units/Optical Network Terminals (ONUs/ONTs) through a passive splitter. ONUs and ONTs are basically the same; an ONU is typically installed at an enterprise, an apartment, or a Multiple Dwelling Unit (MDU) to serve FTTB/FTTN services, while an ONT is typically installed at home to serve FTTH service. ONU is typically called a "Fiber Optic Modem".

\textbf{Downstream Traffic (OLT $\rightarrow$ ONU/ONT)} is broadcast over the passive splitter. 


\textbf{Upstream Traffic (ONU/ONT $\rightarrow$ OLT)} is TDMA based, where each ONU/ONT transmits in its assigned time slot~\cite{novelapon}. 



\subsection{PON Frame Structure}
Major PON standards by ITU-T carry user traffic using two encapsulation methods. GPON uses GPON Encapsulation Method (GEM), and XG-PON, XGS-PON, NG-PON2, and HSP use XG-PON Encapsulation Method (XGEM), both of which carry user Ethernet frames as their payload~\cite{itu-g9843,itu-XGPON,itu-XGSPON,itu-NGPON2,itu-50GPON}.

At the Transmission Convergence (TC) layer, multiple GEM/XGEM frames are then carried in the payload section of TC-layer frames, such as GTC frames in GPON, XGTC frames in XG-PON, and framing sublayer (FS) frames in NG-PON2, XGS-PON and HSPON.

Both NG-PON2 and HSP support time and wavelength division multiplexing (TWDM) mode ~\cite[\S 8.1, \S 1]{itu-NGPON2,itu-50GPON} in addition to TDM mode.


\section{Potential Threats in PON}
Current PON specifications from ITU-T~\cite{itu-g9843,itu-XGPON,itu-XGSPON,itu-NGPON2,itu-50GPON} primarily focused on GEM/XGEM payload confidentiality. As a result, the payload is encrypted, but the header remains in plaintext. (Table~\ref{tab:Encryption-PON})

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Header.}
The two encapsulation methods (GEM, XGEM) expose different fields in plaintext to an adversary 
sharing the splitter. 
\textbf{GEM} carries a 12-bit PLI that reveals payload length, and a 12-bit Port-ID that identifies the logical connection.. 
\textbf{XGEM} carries a 14-bit PLI that reveals payload length , and a 16-bit Port-ID that identifies the logical connection.. 


%Each frame's header contains payload length information. Recent studies show that such payload length information could be exploited to infer user's traffic which means an adversary who shares same splitter as victim can leak user traffic by just receiving optical signals from same splitter and there is no neccessity for an adversary to install in-line optical tap because all downstream traffic is broadcast over PON~\cite{PLI}.

\noindent\textbf{Threat Model.} We consider an adversary that uses a modified ONU~\cite[\S Section 12.1: Basic threat model, \S15.1]{itu-g9843,itu-50GPON} or a commercial PON capture device~\cite{MT2} attached to the victim's splitter. The adversary does not need to install an in-line optical tap or access infrastructure. The adversary simply receives the same downstream optical signals broadcast to the victim~\cite{PLI}.For TWDM Mode, we assume that the adversary can capture the victim's active downstream wavelength channel.



\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Privacy Threat.} Recent work~\cite{PLI} show that the PLI can be exploited to 
infer encrypted streaming traffic on GPON. Beyond per frame length inference, the Port-ID remains constant for the lifetime of a logical connection, allowing the adversary to correlate observations across time and build per-ONU traffic dataset for long-term tracking. The same architectural vulnerability exists in XG-PON, XGS-PON, NG-PON2, and HSP~\cite{itu-XGPON,itu-XGSPON,itu-NGPON2,itu-50GPON}: their XGEM framing header also carries PLI and Port-ID. Concealing the identifier is the main focus of SecurePON.

\section{Challenges}
To realize SecurePON, we modify Higher Speed PON (HSP)~\cite{itu-50GPON} to conceal the XGEM header. Concealing the header requires addressing the following two technical challenges:

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{C1: PLI helps ONU delineate frames.} 
The Payload Length Indicator (PLI) tells the ONU where each XGEM frames ends within the FS payload~\cite[\S 9.2 XGEM frame delineation]{itu-NGPON2}. Encrypting the PLI prevents ONUs from delineating frame boundaries.

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{C2: Port-ID is used for mapping ONU/ONT's logical port.} 
Each ONU filters the downstream XGEM frame by matching Port-ID assigned. Encrypting Port-ID field prevents ONUs from recognizing their own frames.



\section{Proposed Architecture}
\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Design Goals.}
SecurePON periodically rotates the user-data XGEM Port-ID assigned to each ONU. Rotation commands are delivered via the OMCI channel~\cite{itu-50GPON} as an encrypted XGEM payload over the OMCC.
To prevent an adversary on the splitter from linking the retired Port-ID to the new Port-ID via timing correlation, the OLT bursts cover traffic on the retired Port-ID after each rotation. SecurePON addresses C1 and C2 without introducing any new PLOAM message or XGEM header field.

\noindent\textbf{Rotation procedure.} 

\noindent\textbf{Camouflage traffic on retired Port-ID.}
After rotation, the OLT continues to burst downstream XGEM frames bearing the retired Port-ID $X$ for a cover duration $\tau_{\mathrm{cover}} \geq
\tau_{\mathrm{rotation}}$. Cover frames carry encrypted random
padding as their payload, and their PLI values are sampled from the
empirical PLI distribution observed on $X$ during the preceding
window. Because cover and real payloads are encrypted with the same
active unicast key~\cite[\S15.4.1]{itu-g9804-2}, a splitter-resident
adversary cannot statistically distinguish them from header
observations. Consequently, the adversary observes neither an abrupt
termination of traffic on $X$ nor a statistical discontinuity at
the rotation boundary, defeating temporal stitching of $X$ and $Y$
into a single per-ONU PLI sequence.

\noindent\textbf{Scope.} SecurePON targets the downstream broadcast channel, which is the side accessible to a splitter sharing adversary~\cite[\S15.1]{itu-50GPON}. Upstream bursts are isolated by the directional nature of the ODN~\cite[\S12.1]{itu-g9843}.

\noindent\textbf{Limitations.} Typical PON deployments with split ratios of 1:32 to 1:128 offer a
sufficiently large set to prevent the adversary from linking the retired Port-ID to the new Port-ID via timing correlation. In contrast, on a small splitter with only a handful of ONUs (e.g., a 1:2 PON), the anonymity set is too small and Port-ID rotation provides marginal benefit. \textbf{SecurePON} therefore targets deployments of residential PON access (e.g., PON for MDU, Apartments).

\section{Conclusion}
We proposed \textbf{SecurePON}, a security-enhanced PON architecture that periodically rotates the XGEM Port-ID via OMCI and burst cover traffic on expired Port-IDs to prevent passive per-ONU PLI sequence collection at the splitter. By reusing functions already defined in Higher Speed PON~\cite{itu-50GPON}, \textbf{SecurePON} remains compatible with existing deployments. As future work,
